# Prior-release surfaces — the upgrade-path fixture (DEC-110)

`v0_8_0/` is the **verbatim shim surface that forensic-deepdive 0.8.0 actually wrote** into a target
repo. It was produced by executing `emit/shims.py` **as it exists at the `v0.8.0` git tag**, against
a brief path of `docs/codebase/AGENT_BRIEF.md`:

```
git show v0.8.0:src/forensic_deepdive/emit/shims.py > shims_080.py
# then: write_shims(out_dir, "docs/codebase/AGENT_BRIEF.md")
```

## Do not regenerate this with current code

That is the whole point. A fixture generated by today's emitter — even with fields tweaked to *look*
old — tests today's imagination of the past, not the past. These ten files are historical evidence.
Treat them as read-only.

Two of them carry the exact defect that DEC-108 was written for:

| File | Leaks |
|---|---|
| `.claude/skills/codebase-impact-analysis/SKILL.md` | `DEC-015` |
| `.claude/skills/codebase-refactoring/SKILL.md` | `DEC-012` |

Those are internal ledger IDs from a `DECISIONS.md` that is gitignored and never ships. DEC-107
removed them from emitted output; DEC-108 found that `--refresh-shims` could never actually clear
them from an *upgraded* repo, because the DEC-091 ownership gate looked for a `forensic-deepdive`
fingerprint that no skill body has ever contained. This directory is the repo state that proved it,
reduced to a fixture. It was observed in the wild on `hermes-agent` during the v0.9 findings run.

## Why it exists

Every other test in this suite writes shims into an empty `tmp_path`. That tests the **first** run.
909 tests were green over a flag that was dead for half its targets, because nothing exercised the
**second** run — a repo that already carries a previous release's output. See
`tests/test_upgrade_path.py` for the assertions this fixture supports.

## Adding a newer prior release

When 0.10.0 ships, `v0_9_0/` becomes the more interesting fixture (0.8.0 stays — it is the one with
the known leak). Generate it the same way, from the `v0.9.0` tag, and add it to `PRIOR_RELEASES` in
`tests/test_upgrade_path.py`. The supported-upgrade boundary we actually test is documented there.
